domanda:
Contoso archives quarterly compliance exports in a general-purpose v2 storage account. The exports are rarely read, but when auditors request one it must be returned in milliseconds, so the operations team moves the export blobs to the Cold access tier. You must document the number of days a blob must remain in the Cold tier before it can be deleted or moved to another tier without incurring an early deletion penalty.

What is the minimum recommended data retention period for the Cold tier?
spiegazione:
Correct: 90 days. Microsoft Learn states that data in the Cold tier should be stored for a minimum of 90 days; if a blob is deleted, overwritten, or moved to a different tier before 90 days elapse, a prorated early deletion charge applies.

Why the others are wrong:
- 30 days is the minimum recommended retention period for the Cool tier, not the Cold tier. This is the classic confusion between the two adjacent online tiers.
- 180 days is the minimum retention period for the Archive tier, which is an offline tier.
- 365 days is not a retention period for any access tier. It is the maximum retention period you can configure for blob or container soft delete, which is an unrelated data protection feature.
tags: blob storage,access tiers,cold tier,early deletion,minimum retention

domanda:
A storage administrator reports a problem with a general-purpose v2 storage account named contosoarchive1 that is configured for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS). When she selects a block blob in a container and opens the Change tier pane, only Hot, Cool, and Cold are offered. Attempts to set the Archive tier by using Az PowerShell also fail.

What is the reason that the Archive tier is unavailable?
opzione_a: The Archive tier is supported only for storage accounts that are configured for LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS.
opzione_b: The Archive tier can be assigned only as the default account access tier and never on an individual blob.
opzione_c: A blob must first be moved to the Cold tier and remain there for 90 days before it is eligible for the Archive tier.
opzione_d: Blob versioning must be disabled on the storage account before any blob can be moved to the Archive tier.
spiegazione:
Correct: Only storage accounts configured for LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS support moving blobs to the Archive tier. Microsoft Learn explicitly states that the Archive tier isn't supported for ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS accounts, which is why the option is unavailable on a GZRS account.

Why the others are wrong:
- The reverse is true: Archive is set per blob and is explicitly NOT supported as the default account access tier (only Hot, Cool, or Cold can be the account default).
- There is no requirement to stage a blob through the Cold tier. Set Blob Tier can move a blob directly from Hot to Archive; the tier-change matrix on Learn lists Hot to archive as a supported transition.
- Blob versioning has no bearing on Archive eligibility. Versions of a block blob can themselves be moved to the Archive tier with Set Blob Tier.

domanda:
A legal team needs to analyze a 6-GB block blob named case4471.vhdx that was moved to the Archive tier 40 days ago. The blob must be readable in an online tier, but your manager insists that the operation must not trigger the 180-day early deletion fee on the archived data.

Which action should you perform?
opzione_a: Call Set Blob Tier on case4471.vhdx and specify the Hot tier with a high rehydrate priority.
opzione_b: Call Copy Blob to copy case4471.vhdx to a new blob name in the Hot tier, leaving the source blob in the Archive tier.
opzione_c: Add a lifecycle management rule with a tierToCool action and daysAfterModificationGreaterThan set to 0.
opzione_d: Create a snapshot of case4471.vhdx and call Set Blob Tier on the snapshot to move it to the Hot tier.
spiegazione:
Correct: Copying an archived blob to a new blob in an online tier leaves the source blob unmodified in the Archive tier, so the early deletion fee is never assessed. Microsoft Learn recommends Copy Blob for exactly this reason and notes the copy must target a different blob name or a different container. You are billed for data read transactions, data retrieval, and capacity for both blobs.

Why the others are wrong:
- Set Blob Tier changes the tier of the archived blob itself. Because only 40 of the required 180 days have elapsed, this incurs an early deletion fee equivalent to the remaining 140 days.
- Lifecycle management policies cannot be used to rehydrate blobs from the Archive tier to an online tier at all, so the rule would have no effect on the archived blob.
- Snapshots aren't supported for blobs in the Archive tier, so the snapshot cannot be created. Learn also states that snapshots and previous versions cannot be rehydrated directly.
tags: blob storage,archive tier,rehydration,copy blob,early deletion penalty

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
During a cleanup script test, a developer accidentally ran a Delete Container operation against a container named prod-invoices in a general-purpose v2 storage account. The container and all of its blobs disappeared. Management asks you to make sure that a future accidental container deletion can be reversed for at least 30 days.

What should you configure on the storage account?
opzione_a: Container soft delete with a 30-day retention period
opzione_b: Blob soft delete with a 30-day retention period
opzione_c: Blob versioning, and keep all versions
opzione_d: A CanNotDelete Azure Resource Manager lock on the storage account resource
spiegazione:
Correct: Container soft delete is the only in-account feature that retains a deleted container so that it can be recovered with the Restore Container operation. The retention period is configurable between 1 and 365 days, so 30 days is valid. When a container is restored, its blobs and any versions and snapshots are restored with it.

Why the others are wrong:
- Blob soft delete protects only an individual blob, snapshot, or version. Microsoft Learn is explicit that when a container is deleted, the blobs inside it are not recoverable through blob soft delete.
- Blob versioning cannot help you recover from the accidental deletion of a container or a storage account; it only preserves previous versions of blobs whose parent container still exists.
- An ARM lock on the storage account prevents deletion of the account resource, not of containers created within it, because container deletion is a data-plane operation. It also provides no way to recover a container that was already deleted.
tags: blob storage,container soft delete,data protection,restore container

domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account has blob versioning enabled and blob soft delete enabled with a 7-day retention period. The account does not have a hierarchical namespace. An application calls Delete Blob against a blob named catalog.json without specifying a version ID. Users now report that catalog.json returns 404 Not Found.

You need to make the most recent state of catalog.json available again at its original blob name.

What should you do?
opzione_a: Call Undelete Blob on catalog.json, which promotes the most recent previous version back to the current version.
opzione_b: Call Copy Blob to copy the most recent previous version of catalog.json over the blob name, creating a new current version.
opzione_c: Use container soft delete to restore the parent container within the 7-day retention period.
opzione_d: Call Set Blob Tier on the most recent previous version of catalog.json and specify the Hot tier.
spiegazione:
Correct: When versioning and soft delete are both enabled and you delete a blob without a version ID, the current version simply becomes a previous version and there is no longer a current version. All previous versions persist and are not soft-deleted. Microsoft Learn states that to restore the current version you must promote a previous version by copying it with Copy Blob, which creates a new current version.

Why the others are wrong:
- Undelete Blob restores soft-deleted versions or snapshots but explicitly does not restore the current version. In this scenario no version was soft-deleted at all, so Undelete Blob would have no useful effect.
- Container soft delete restores whole containers. The container here was never deleted, and Learn warns that container soft delete cannot be used to restore an individual blob when the parent container still exists.
- Set Blob Tier only changes the access tier of a version. It does not promote a previous version to be the current version, so catalog.json would still return 404.
tags: blob storage,blob versioning,soft delete,undelete blob,copy blob,promote version

domanda:
A storage account has a lifecycle management policy whose only rule applies a tierToArchive action to block blobs when daysAfterModificationGreaterThan is 365. An engineer rehydrates several archived blobs to the Hot tier by calling Set Blob Tier because a project restarted. Within 24 hours, every rehydrated blob is back in the Archive tier, even though the engineer is actively reading them.

You need to prevent the policy from returning rehydrated blobs to the Archive tier for 30 days after rehydration, while keeping the existing archiving behavior for all other blobs.

What should you do?
opzione_a: Add the daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan condition set to 30 to the tierToArchive action.
opzione_b: Increase daysAfterModificationGreaterThan on the tierToArchive action from 365 to 395.
opzione_c: Enable last access time tracking and replace daysAfterModificationGreaterThan with daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan set to 30 on the tierToArchive action.
opzione_d: Add the enableAutoTierToHotFromCool action to the rule.
spiegazione:
Correct: Rehydrating a blob does not update its last modified time, so the blob still satisfies daysAfterModificationGreaterThan and the policy re-archives it. Microsoft Learn documents daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan as the condition that specifies the minimum number of days a rehydrated blob is kept in an online tier before being returned to Archive, and it applies only to tierToArchive actions. Setting it to 30 gives exactly the required 30-day grace period.

Why the others are wrong:
- Raising daysAfterModificationGreaterThan to 395 only delays archiving for blobs modified less than 395 days ago. The rehydrated blobs were last modified far longer ago, so they would still be re-archived on the next run.
- daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan is a valid condition, but it changes the archiving criteria for every blob the rule matches, which violates the requirement to keep the existing behavior for other blobs. Learn specifically prescribes daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan for the rehydration scenario.
- enableAutoTierToHotFromCool moves blobs from Cool to Hot when accessed. It requires the daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan condition and does nothing for blobs being tiered to Archive.

domanda:
You are creating a blob container in the Azure portal to hold web server logs. The New container pane rejects the name you type.

Which container name is valid?
spiegazione:
Correct: archive-logs-2026 satisfies every rule. Microsoft Learn states that a container name must be lowercase, must start with a letter or number, may contain only letters, numbers, and the dash (-) character, and must be between 3 and 63 characters long.

Why the others are wrong:
- Archive-Logs contains uppercase letters. Container names must be all lowercase.
- ab is only 2 characters. The minimum length is 3 characters.
- archive_logs uses an underscore. Only letters, numbers, and the dash character are permitted.

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
You are documenting the behavior of blob soft delete for a general-purpose v2 storage account that does not have a hierarchical namespace.

Which three statements are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: The soft delete retention period can be set to any value between 1 and 365 days.
opzione_b: Blob soft delete does not protect against deletion of the storage account; an Azure Resource Manager lock on the account resource is required for that.
opzione_c: Data in a page blob that is overwritten by the Put Page operation can be recovered by using blob soft delete.
opzione_d: Soft-deleted data is billed at the same rate as active data.
opzione_e: Shortening the retention period causes objects that were already soft-deleted to expire sooner, based on the new value.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
- The retention period for soft-deleted objects is specified as a value between 1 and 365 days, exactly as documented on Microsoft Learn.
- Learn states plainly that blob soft delete does not protect against the deletion of a storage account and recommends configuring a lock on the storage account resource for that scenario.
- All soft-deleted data is billed at the same rate as active data; you are only relieved of the charge once the object is permanently deleted after the retention period elapses.

Why the others are wrong:
- Put Page is explicitly listed as "no change" in the soft delete protection matrix. Page blob data that is overwritten or cleared with Put Page isn't saved and isn't recoverable, which is why soft delete cannot undo writes made by an Azure VM to an unmanaged disk.
- An updated retention period applies only to data deleted after the change. Any data deleted before the change remains subject to the retention period that was in effect at the time it was deleted, and attempting to delete a soft-deleted object doesn't affect its expiry time.
tags: blob storage,blob soft delete,retention period,put page,billing,resource lock

domanda:
Before rolling out lifecycle management policies across several general-purpose v2 storage accounts, you must brief the operations team on the documented constraints of the feature.

Which three statements are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A lifecycle management policy can rehydrate blobs from the Archive tier to the Hot tier when a matching rule is evaluated.
opzione_b: If a rule applies the prefixMatch filter, it can define up to 10 case-sensitive prefixes.
opzione_c: A single lifecycle management policy can define up to 100 rules.
opzione_d: Tiering actions such as tierToCool are supported for append blobs and page blobs in a general-purpose v2 account.
opzione_e: The delete action of a lifecycle management policy has no effect on a blob that is in an immutable container.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
- Microsoft Learn states that each rule can define up to 10 case-sensitive prefixes when the prefixMatch filter is applied. The same limit of 10 conditions applies to the blobIndexMatch filter.
- The rules array requires at least one rule and you can define up to 100 rules in a policy.
- The delete action won't work with any blob in an immutable container, because a time-based retention policy or legal hold allows objects to be created and read but not modified or deleted.

Why the others are wrong:
- Lifecycle management policies explicitly cannot be used to rehydrate blobs to an online tier. Rehydration must be performed with Set Blob Tier or Copy Blob.
- Tiering is allowed only on block blobs, not on append or page blobs, and tiering isn't supported at all in a premium block blob storage account. The blobTypes filter itself accepts only blockBlob or appendBlob, and append blobs can be targeted only by actions such as delete.

domanda:
Your organization keeps long-term backups in the Archive tier of a GRS general-purpose v2 storage account. You are preparing a runbook that describes how operators retrieve archived data during an incident.

Which three statements about blob rehydration are accurate? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: A standard-priority rehydration request might take up to 15 hours to complete for objects under 10 GB in size.
opzione_b: While a standard-priority rehydration is pending, you can raise the rehydration priority to High, but you cannot lower a pending High-priority request back to Standard.
opzione_c: After a Set Blob Tier rehydration request is initiated, you can cancel it while it's still in progress.
opzione_d: Starting with service version 2021-02-12, you can rehydrate an archived blob by copying it to a different storage account, as long as the destination account is in the same region as the source account.
opzione_e: A blob snapshot or a previous version that is in the Archive tier can be rehydrated directly to the Hot tier by calling Set Blob Tier on it.
spiegazione:
Correct answers:
- Microsoft Learn defines standard priority as processed in the order received, possibly taking up to 15 hours to complete for objects under 10 GB. High priority might complete in less than one hour for objects under 10 GB.
- Learn states that while a standard-priority rehydration is pending you can update the setting to High to rehydrate the blob more quickly, and that the rehydration priority setting can't be lowered from High to Standard for a pending operation.
- Before service version 2021-02-12 rehydration by copy was supported only within the same storage account. From 2021-02-12 onward you can copy to a different storage account provided it's in the same region, which lets you segregate production and backup data.

Why the others are wrong:
- Once a Set Blob Tier request is initiated, it can't be canceled. During the operation the blob's access tier continues to show as archived until rehydration completes.
- Snapshots and previous versions cannot be rehydrated back to an online tier directly. To access data from an archived snapshot or previous version, you must copy it to a new blob in an online tier with the Copy Blob operation.
tags: blob storage,archive tier,rehydration priority,set blob tier,copy blob,snapshots

domanda:
Fabrikam must retain diagnostic exports in a general-purpose v2 storage account that is configured for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS). The exports are read only two or three times a year, but each read must return the first byte within milliseconds. Fabrikam wants the lowest possible storage capacity cost that still meets the latency requirement, and new blobs uploaded to the account must land in that tier automatically without the upload code specifying a tier.

Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Access tier to apply to the export blobs: [Cool | Cold | Archive]
opzione_b: Minimum recommended retention period before an early deletion penalty applies to those blobs: [30 days | 90 days | 180 days]
opzione_c: Default account access tier setting to configure on the storage account: [Cold | Archive | Cannot be configured for this tier]
spiegazione:
Dropdown 1 - Cold: The Cold tier is an online tier optimized for data that is rarely accessed but still requires fast retrieval, with lower storage costs than Cool. Cool also meets the millisecond latency requirement but costs more to store, so Cold is the lowest-cost option that qualifies. Archive is wrong twice over: it's an offline tier with retrieval latency measured in hours, and it isn't supported on GZRS accounts at all.

Dropdown 2 - 90 days: Data in the Cold tier should be stored for a minimum of 90 days or a prorated early deletion charge applies. 30 days is the Cool tier minimum and 180 days is the Archive tier minimum.

Dropdown 3 - Cold: The default account access tier setting determines the online tier in which a new blob is created when the upload doesn't specify one, and it can be set to Hot, Cool, or Cold. Setting it to Cold satisfies the requirement that new blobs land in the correct tier automatically. The Archive tier is explicitly not supported as the default access tier for a storage account, and the setting is certainly configurable for Cold, so the third option is incorrect.
tags: blob storage,access tiers,cold tier,default access tier,gzrs,early deletion

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
You are reviewing the Data protection blade of a general-purpose v2 storage account and must record the configurable boundaries of the soft delete features for a design document.

Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Minimum retention period that can be configured for blob soft delete: [1 day | 7 days | 14 days]
opzione_b: Maximum retention period that can be configured for container soft delete: [90 days | 365 days | 3,650 days]
opzione_c: Default retention period for container soft delete: [1 day | 7 days | 30 days]
spiegazione:
Dropdown 1 - 1 day: When you enable blob soft delete you specify a retention period for deleted objects of between 1 and 365 days, so 1 day is the minimum you can configure. 7 days is only the minimum retention period that Microsoft recommends, not a hard floor, and 14 days is not a boundary of the feature.

Dropdown 2 - 365 days: Container soft delete uses the same 1 to 365 day range as blob soft delete, so 365 days is the maximum. 90 days is the Cold tier minimum retention period, not a soft delete boundary, and 3,650 days is not a valid soft delete value.

Dropdown 3 - 7 days: Microsoft Learn states that the default retention period for container soft delete is seven days and recommends a minimum of seven days, increasing it as needed based on data volume and how long it may take to detect a data-loss event.
tags: blob storage,blob soft delete,container soft delete,retention period,data protection

domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account has blob versioning enabled. Auditors require that previous versions of block blobs be permanently removed 90 days after the version itself was first written, while the current version of each blob remains untouched. You are building the lifecycle management rule that implements this.

Select the appropriate option for each dropdown.
opzione_a: blobTypes filter value to specify: [blockBlob | appendBlob | pageBlob]
opzione_b: Section of the rule definition that the Delete action must be placed under: [baseBlob | snapshot | version]
opzione_c: Run condition to pair with the Delete action: [daysAfterModificationGreaterThan | daysAfterCreationGreaterThan | daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan]
spiegazione:
Dropdown 1 - blockBlob: The blobTypes filter is required and accepts only blockBlob or appendBlob. The requirement names block blobs, so blockBlob is correct. pageBlob isn't a valid blobTypes value at all, and appendBlob would not match the target data.

Dropdown 2 - version: A policy can operate on current versions, previous versions, and snapshots. Placing the Delete action under version targets previous versions only, leaving the current version untouched as required. Putting it under baseBlob would delete the current version, and snapshot targets manually created snapshots rather than versions.

Dropdown 3 - daysAfterCreationGreaterThan: Microsoft Learn states that rules for previous versions use the creation time of that version when the blob was first written, not when the version became a previous version, and that daysAfterCreationGreaterThan applies to actions on the current version, the previous version, or a snapshot. daysAfterModificationGreaterThan applies only to actions on a current version. daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan applies only to tierToArchive actions, not to Delete.

Note that a lifecycle policy will not delete the current version of a blob until any previous versions or snapshots associated with it have been deleted.

sotto_argomento: Configure soft delete for blobs and containers
domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account named contosodata7 does not have a hierarchical namespace. Blob soft delete is enabled with a retention period of 14 days. Container soft delete is not enabled, and blob versioning is not enabled.

Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true for this configuration.

1. If a user calls Delete Container on a container in contosodata7, the container and its blobs can be restored within 14 days.
2. If an application overwrites an existing block blob by calling Put Blob, a soft-deleted snapshot capturing the blob's state prior to the write is created automatically.
3. If a user deletes the contosodata7 storage account resource, the blobs it contained can be recovered within 14 days.
opzione_a: If a user calls Delete Container on a container in contosodata7, the container and its blobs can be restored within 14 days.
opzione_b: If an application overwrites an existing block blob by calling Put Blob, a soft-deleted snapshot capturing the blob's state prior to the write is created automatically.
opzione_c: If a user deletes the contosodata7 storage account resource, the blobs it contained can be recovered within 14 days.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 - No: Blob soft delete protects an individual blob, snapshot, or version. The protection matrix on Microsoft Learn lists Delete Container as "No change. Blobs in the deleted container aren't recoverable." Restoring a deleted container requires container soft delete, which is not enabled here.

Statement 2 - Yes: When blob soft delete is enabled on an account without a hierarchical namespace, overwriting a blob with Put Blob, Put Block List, or Copy Blob automatically creates a soft-deleted snapshot of the blob's state prior to the write operation. That snapshot is permanently deleted when the 14-day retention period expires. This behavior applies because versioning is not enabled; with versioning enabled a new version would be created instead.

Statement 3 - No: Learn states explicitly that blob soft delete does not protect against the deletion of a storage account, and that containers and blobs in a deleted account aren't recoverable. To protect the account itself you must configure an Azure Resource Manager lock on the storage account resource.
tags: blob storage,blob soft delete,soft-deleted snapshot,delete container,storage account deletion

domanda:
A general-purpose v2 storage account named fabrikamdocs has blob versioning enabled and blob soft delete enabled with a 7-day retention period. The account does not have a hierarchical namespace and has no object replication policies.

Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true for this configuration.

1. When an application overwrites a block blob with Put Block List, a new version is created and no soft-deleted snapshot is created.
2. If an administrator calls Delete Blob and specifies the version ID of a previous version, that version is soft-deleted and is permanently removed after 7 days.
3. If you disable blob versioning on fabrikamdocs, the versions that already exist are deleted from the storage account.
opzione_a: When an application overwrites a block blob with Put Block List, a new version is created and no soft-deleted snapshot is created.
opzione_b: If an administrator calls Delete Blob and specifies the version ID of a previous version, that version is soft-deleted and is permanently removed after 7 days.
opzione_c: If you disable blob versioning on fabrikamdocs, the versions that already exist are deleted from the storage account.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 - Yes: Microsoft Learn states that if blob versioning and blob soft delete are both enabled, overwriting a blob automatically creates a new previous version that reflects the blob's state before the write operation, and no soft-deleted snapshots are created. The new version isn't soft-deleted and isn't removed when the soft-delete retention period expires. Put Block List is one of the write operations that triggers version creation.

Statement 2 - Yes: To delete a previous version you call Delete Blob and specify the version ID. Soft delete offers additional protection for blob versions: the deleted version becomes soft-deleted and is preserved until the soft delete retention period elapses, at which point it's permanently deleted. Note that deleting a previous version requires the Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/deleteBlobVersion/action data action, granted by Storage Blob Data Owner.

Statement 3 - No: Disabling blob versioning doesn't delete existing blobs, versions, or snapshots. Existing versions remain accessible and can still be read, listed, or deleted by version ID; only new version creation stops. (Object replication relies on versioning, so any object replication policies would have to be deleted before versioning could be disabled, but the account has none.)
tags: blob storage,blob versioning,soft delete,delete blob version,disable versioning

domanda:
Northwind stores contract documents as block blobs in a general-purpose v2 storage account. Compliance requires that every change to a contract be retained, and that superseded copies be purged automatically 180 days after they were first written. Neither blob versioning nor any lifecycle management policy is currently configured on the account.

You need to implement the requirement by using the Azure portal.

Drag the four actions into the correct order.
opzione_a: In the rule's blob subtype configuration, select Previous versions and add a Delete action with daysAfterCreationGreaterThan set to 180.
opzione_b: On the Data protection blade of the storage account, select Enable versioning for blobs.
opzione_c: Save the policy, then allow up to 24 hours for the change to take effect and for the first policy run to start.
opzione_d: On the Lifecycle management blade, add a rule and set the blob type filter to Block blobs.
spiegazione:
Correct order: b, d, a, c.

1. Enable versioning for blobs on the Data protection blade (b). Versioning must exist before a rule can act on previous versions. Once enabled, every write operation to a blob creates a new version, so the superseded copies the rule will later delete only start accumulating from this point. Blobs created before versioning was enabled do not have a version ID.

2. Add a lifecycle management rule and set the blob type filter to Block blobs (d). The blobTypes filter is a required element of every rule and must be set before the actions can be defined; it accepts blockBlob or appendBlob.

3. Configure the Delete action under Previous versions with daysAfterCreationGreaterThan set to 180 (a). Rules for previous versions use the creation time of that version when the blob was first written, which is exactly what the compliance requirement specifies, so daysAfterCreationGreaterThan is the correct run condition.

4. Save the policy and wait (c). Microsoft Learn states that when you add or edit the rules of a lifecycle policy, it can take up to 24 hours for changes to go into effect and for the first execution to start, so this step is necessarily last.

A common error is reversing steps 1 and 2: creating the lifecycle rule first leaves nothing for the Previous versions action to target, because no versions are being generated yet. Note also that enabling the "Delete versions after" option directly on the Data protection blade would auto-create a lifecycle rule, but it doesn't provide the block-blob filtering shown here.
tags: blob storage,lifecycle management,blob versioning,delete previous versions,azure portal,policy execution
